1:
The date in the first verse has to be reconciled with the murder of Pekah seven or eight years earlier. Gill offers an interregnum, or else that Hoshea was not generally acknowledged until then. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that he usurped the kingdom in the fourth year of Ahaz but was not established in it until the twelfth. Ellicott recomputes instead: if Pekah reigned thirty years and Ahaz succeeded in Pekah's seventeenth, then Ahaz reigned thirteen years concurrently with Pekah and Hoshea succeeded in his fourteenth year;; the inscription of Tiglath Pileser makes Hoshea an Assyrian vassal from the first. Henry reads the delay morally, that he was justly kept from the throne he had aimed at, and that the word of Hosea was fulfilled, now they shall say, We have no king.

That he was not as the kings before him is agreed and then qualified. Gill and Wesley say he neither served Baal nor could serve the calves, one of them having been carried off already,. Ellicott doubts that he abandoned the Bethel worship and allows only that he may have discountenanced the Baals and the Asheras, remarking that the last sovereigns of falling monarchies have not always been the worst of their line. Henry presses the difficulty this creates, that the ruin came in the reign of one of the better kings, and answers that God was reckoning the iniquities of the foregoing ages and the sins of the people, whose king gave them leave to do better and who did as badly as ever.

The identity of the conqueror is disputed. Clarke and Gill make Shalmaneser the son and successor of Tiglath-pileser, Clarke adding that Hosea calls him Shalman and Tobit Enemessar. Wesley notes that the older Hebrew writers identified him with Sennacherib, since one man in the East may carry several names. Keil and Delitzsch go further and make him the Sargon of Isaiah, whose name is spelt Sargina on the monuments. Ellicott keeps them apart as Shalmaneser the Fourth and his successor, notes that no annals of his reign survive, and observes that the narrative never says Shalmaneser besieged Samaria three years and took it, since Sargon claims the capture in his own first year.

On the Egyptian alliance the commentators converge. Keil and Delitzsch take So for one of the two Shebeks of the Ethiopian dynasty without settling which. Ellicott points the name Sewe, identifies him with Shabaka whom Sargon defeated at Raphia, and observes that Sargon calls him a prince rather than a king, Lower Egypt being then divided among petty principalities, so that the alliance was worth little; he also corrects brought to offered, the word being used elsewhere of sacrifice, and infers from the shutting up that Hoshea was taken before the siege began. Henry calls Egypt a broken reed and says that men get nothing by struggling with the net but entangle themselves the more.

The places of exile are read two ways. Keil and Delitzsch insist the text puts them in provinces of Assyria and Media and not in Mesopotamia; Ellicott identifies Halah with the Assyrian Halahhu and places it in Mesopotamia beside Rezeph and Gozan, reading on Habor the river of Gozan. Ellicott also quotes from Botta the tally Sargon claims, twenty-seven thousand two hundred and eighty carried off. Clarke observes that a city holding out three years must have been well fortified and provisioned, cites Hosea and Micah for the cruelties done when it fell, and argues at length, following Sir William Jones, that the Afghans are the descendants of the captive tribes. Wesley closes as Henry does, that they who forgot God were themselves forgotten, and they who studied to be like the nations were buried among them.
7:
The historian turns from the event to its causes, and the commentators mark how deliberately. Keil and Delitzsch take the opening words as and it came to pass when rather than because, so that the sentence does not close until the eighteenth verse, everything between being an explanation of the sin. Henry notices what is passed over: the weakness of Israel, the mismanagement of her kings, the growing strength of Assyria, none of these are allowed to stand as the reason, since the Assyrian was but the rod of his anger. He refuses to let the ruin be called a bare act of sovereignty and calls it an act of necessary justice. Gill says simply that the sin enlarged on through the whole discourse is idolatry.

What God had given is set against what they did. Henry lists three gifts that bound them: their liberty out of the hand of Pharaoh, their law with God himself for king, and their land, emptied of nations whose casting out was itself the plainest warning. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both find the guilt twofold, idolatry in the strict sense and a heathenish way of worshipping Jehovah himself under the form of a bullock, which is what the statutes of the kings of Israel means. Henry observes that nothing but the idolatry is specified here, though they had broken all the commands of the second table, because this was the spiritual adultery that broke the marriage covenant and let in the rest.

The clause rendered did secretly divides them sharply. Keil and Delitzsch follow Hengstenberg in taking it of covering words that were not right concerning Jehovah, an attempt to conceal the true nature of the revealed God by arbitrary perversions of his word, and reject both the reading that they trifled with such things and the reading that they dealt perfidiously. Ellicott takes the second of these, noting that the literal sense is covered and that Hebrew verbs of covering and hiding are often used of dealing treacherously, and that the form here occurs nowhere else. Gill and Wesley allow either that they were ashamed to own such practices openly, or that they covered the worship of the calves with plausible pretences. Henry reads the secrecy as evidence of their atheism, that they thought what was done in secret was out from under God's eye.

On the spread of the high places all agree and each adds a detail. Clarke says the idolatry was universal, from the largest city to the smallest village and from the public watchtower to the shepherd's cot. Ellicott contrasts the solitary buildings tenanted by a few herdsmen with the embattled cities that protected multitudes, so that wherever men were, in small numbers or large, a high place was established. Wesley reaches the same point from the other side, that they were set up even in the most uninhabited parts. Henry puts the reason under it: having forsaken the one place God had chosen, they knew no end of high places.

The images and the idols are named with contempt. Ellicott calls them pillars and Asheras, sacred trunks,; Clarke identifies the groves with the rites of Ashtaroth. Gill observes that groves of trees could not be set under green trees, so that idols of stone and wood must be meant, and remarks that the Indians still place idols in little groves or at the foot of a hill that casts a shadow. On the last verse Ellicott renders the word the dunglings, a term of contempt; Keil and Delitzsch render it the clods, masses of stone worshipped as gods; and Gill, taking it the same way, notes that Sterculius was a name of Saturn, given him for finding out how to make land fruitful with dung.
13:
The warning is described before the refusal. Ellicott would render the verb adjured rather than testified against, a solemn charge rather than an accusation, and notes that the Hebrew reads by the hand of all his prophets, every seer, where the Syriac and the Vulgate make both nouns plural. He distinguishes the seers as men who did not belong to the prophetic order but came forward in an emergency on a sudden divine impulse; Wesley describes them by what they received rather than what they were, men to whom God declared his mind by revelations and visions and whose word was borne witness to from heaven. Gill supplies the names, Ahijah the Shilonite, Elijah and Elisha, Hosea, Amos and Micah. Clarke says it is this succession that leaves the conduct inexcusable, since the prophets preached not only repentance but God's readiness to forgive if they would return.

Why Judah is named here at all is a question both the critics answer. Keil and Delitzsch say the historian mentions Judah while describing the causes of Israel's rejection in order to indicate beforehand that Judah was preparing the same fate for itself, as the nineteenth verse says plainly. Ellicott reaches a similar place by a different route, that both kingdoms apostatised and prophets were sent to both, and both reject the suggestion that the reference is to the time before the partition of the kingdom. Ellicott adds a smaller correction, that since the prophets did not bring the law but interpreted it, the closing clause is better read according to all that I sent to you by my servants the prophets.

The refusal is put in one image. Ellicott reads simply and they hearkened not, notes that neck is singular and that the Greek and Syriac read more than the neck of their fathers, one letter differing in the Hebrew, and insists that the unbelief charged is moral rather than intellectual, unbelief showing itself as disobedience, so that what they withheld was the obedience of faith. Wesley makes the same point from the figure, that they refused to submit the neck to the yoke of God's precepts, a metaphor from stubborn oxen.

Following vanity is read as a judgment on the whole life. Keil and Delitzsch note that the phrase stands word for word in Jeremiah and take it as a description of the worthlessness of their whole aim in the one thing that matters, since whatever a man sets before him apart from God leads to spiritual and moral corruption. Ellicott gives the word its root sense, a breath, and then whatever is as transient as a breath, the idols and their worship being meant here. Wesley presses the consequence, that by long worship of idols they were made like them, vain and senseless creatures. Gill draws the legal conclusion, that he who offends in one point is guilty of all.

The climax is the list itself. Keil and Delitzsch observe that worship of the host of heaven is nowhere else charged against the ten tribes and appears first in Judah under Manasseh, and that its position between the Asherah and Baal shows the expression borrowed from Deuteronomy to mark the character of that worship. Ellicott, quoting Schlottmann at length, takes the Asherah for the commonest material representation of Astarte herself, a real trunk planted in the ground, rootless but not branchless, signifying nature or the world set beside Baal the lord of the world. Wesley names the host plainly as the stars. Gill takes Baal and Moloch for one, representing the sun which presides in the element of fire, and leaves open whether the children were passed through it in lustration or burnt; Clarke says of the last clause that they abandoned themselves to work all iniquity with greediness.
18:
Who was left is stated narrowly and then widened. Ellicott takes the tribe to mean the kingdom, and reads removed them out of his sight as an expression founded on the old local conceptions of deity, banishment from his land being banishment from his presence. Clarke reckons under the name of Judah all of Benjamin and Levi and those Israelites who abandoned their idolatries and joined themselves to Judah, since it was the ten tribes only that Assyria carried away; Wesley counts the same, the greater part of Benjamin with those of Simeon and Levi who had been incorporated. Clarke adds what the banishment cost them, the promised land, the temple, and every ordinance of righteousness at once.

The complaint against Judah is read as an aggravation of Israel's guilt. Gill and Wesley both say that Judah was drawn in by the example of the ten tribes and persisted even after seeing what befell them, so that Israel's sin was not only evil in itself but mischievous to a neighbour instructed by it. Ellicott makes Judah no real or permanent exception to the sins or the punishment, names Ahaziah and Ahaz as the kings who especially favoured the northern worship, and says the example of her more powerful neighbour exercised a fatally powerful spell.

How far the rejection reaches is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch take all the seed of Israel for the whole nation and not merely the ten tribes, and separate two things the narrative keeps close together: rejection, which consisted in chastisement and deliverance into the hand of plunderers, penal judgments by which the Lord sought to bring them back and to keep them from being driven among the heathen; and the thrusting from his face, which is exile itself. Ellicott holds that Israel is used in the narrow sense in these verses, takes the spoilers for the Syrians and the Assyrians, and thinks the writer had the language of Judges in mind. Gill puts the same rejection in the prophets' terms, that a Lo-ammi was written on them and a bill of divorce given.

The rending of the kingdom produces the sharpest division in the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch hold that Jehovah is the subject, since the ellipsis required by the other reading is too harsh and since it is God who is said elsewhere to have rent the kingdom from Solomon, while nowhere is Israel said to have rent it from the house of David. Ellicott answers that the Hebrew as it stands can only mean Israel rent, there being no object after the transitive verb, and prefers to restore the passive, Israel rent himself away, with the Vulgate. Gill keeps the act with the Lord, as done according to his purpose and his prophecy; Wesley lays the making of Jeroboam king on the people, who would not wait until God had invested him with what he had promised. Ellicott sees in the verse the source of the whole evil, separation from Judah leading to the calf worship and that to idolatry outright, and Wesley notes that the great sin is so called to meet the conceit of Israelites who thought it small because their kings compelled it.

The close is guarded on both sides. Ellicott observes that the land was not wholly emptied, as later chronicles show, but that the distinctive character of the nation was lost, those who remained becoming mixed with their heathen neighbours. Keil and Delitzsch enter a caution about the phrase unto this day, that the Hebrew particle is not always exclusive, so that nothing can be inferred from it either for or against a later return of the ten tribes.
24:
Which king resettled the land is not agreed. Ellicott names Sargon, who records in his own annals that in his first year he settled conquered Babylonians in Syria and in his seventh caused certain Arab tribes to dwell in the city of Samerina, the very phrase the verse uses; Esarhaddon, on his reading, only reinforced the colony later. Keil and Delitzsch argue it cannot be Shalmaneser, since a considerable period plainly intervened between the deportation and the resettlement, and take it for Esarhaddon on the evidence of Ezra. Gill allows Shalmaneser but inclines to Esarhaddon as well. Clarke explains the policy rather than the man: one people is removed entire and another substituted, the newcomers having no patrimony in the land worth contending for.

The places are identified by philology and by excavation in turn. Clarke derives Cuthah from Cush, and notes that the Samaritans were therefore called Cuthaeans and their speech Cuthite; he takes the Avim for the people expelled by the Caphtorim. Ellicott reaches the same towns from the inscriptions: Kutie with its temple of Nergal, whose ruins were found at Tell-Ibrahim, and Sipar, the two Sipars, named for the sun and for Anunit, whose great sun temple Rassam uncovered. Henry stands back from all of it, that never was land lost for want of an heir, and that it is sad for the holy land to become heathen again.

The lions divide the natural account from the providential. Clarke says wild beasts would necessarily increase in a land emptied of its people, without any supernatural intervention, and that the newcomers supposed a plague because they thought, as heathens did, that every district has its tutelary deity; yet he ends by allowing that God likely did send them as a scourge. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch give the same natural cause, the lions having multiplied while the land lay waste, and both observe that the sacred writer himself endorses the colonists' reading of the visitation, remembering the threat in Leviticus. Henry presses the hand of God further, that the rough welcome was meant to check their insolence and to teach them that though they had conquered Israel, the God of Israel had power enough to deal with them. Wesley adds that the neglect was strange even by heathen standards, since men commonly worshipped the gods of the country they came into.

Their appeal to the king is read as a reproach to Israel. Henry observes that they were readier to hear the voice of God's judgments than Israel had been, so that Assyrians begged to be taught what Israelites hated to be taught. Ellicott would render it men spake rather than they spake and takes the manner of the God of the land for his appointed worship; Clarke gives the same sense, the judgment, the way he is to be worshipped.

The priest sent back is judged by where he settled. Gill reports that an Arabic writer calls him Uzziah and Epiphanius Esdras, and concludes he was doubtless one of the priests of the calves, since no others had been carried away, and since he chose Bethel, where he had probably officiated before. Ellicott agrees on both grounds and adds that he was teaching, a permanent work, and that fearing the Lord is meant here in the old ceremonial and not the modern ethical sense; Wesley infers the same from the manner of making priests that followed. Henry says a prophet would have done them more good, and that though this man might teach them to do better he was not likely to teach them to do well. Clarke alone looks forward, that imperfect as the teaching was it ended by overthrowing their idolatry, and adds that the remnant in his own day was some thirty families at Naplouse and Jaffa, who kept their synagogue and went to it in white robes.
29:
What the colonists did with the teaching is stated first. Ellicott would begin the verse with a plain and rather than howbeit, and says they did not fear Jehovah in any monotheistic sense but simply added his worship to that of their ancestral gods; the houses of the high places are the shrines that served the several cities. Gill notes that the newcomers set their own images in the places Israel had built for idolatry, and Clarke that the gods they made were copies of what they had worshipped at home.

The list of idols is where the commentators separate. For Succoth-benoth, Gill and Clarke both take the name as booths of the daughters and refer it to the prostitution of women at the temple of the Babylonian Venus which Herodotus describes, Clarke deriving the very name Venus from benoth; Gill reports besides the rabbinic figure of a hen and chickens and a guess at the Pleiades. Ellicott thinks the spelling has suffered in transmission and identifies the goddess Zarpanitum, the seed-maker, consort of Merodach. For Nergal, Clarke offers the solar orb with a cock for emblem; Ellicott points to the colossal lions that guarded Assyrian doorways, which were called nirgali, and to a syllabary naming Nergal the god of Kutha. For Ashima, Clarke guesses at fire from a root meaning to make atonement, while Ellicott says nothing is known of it and rejects the identification with the Phoenician Eshmun.

Nibhaz and Tartak are read three ways. Gill and Clarke follow the rabbis in giving the first the shape of a dog, from the root meaning to bark, and identifying it with the barking Anubis, and the second the shape of an ass; Clarke describes a stone image of the kind lying before him as he wrote, seven inches high, with the body of a man and the head and feet of a dog. Gill adds a wholly different derivation, that Nibhaz means the remote one seeth, and so the sun, while Tartak is a chain and may denote the fixed stars chained in their places. Keil and Delitzsch report the same rabbinic figures but prefer the view that makes both infernal powers, Tartak a demon of the lower regions from a word for deep darkness and Nibhaz a dreadful king of the underworld. Ellicott declines all of it, saying the two are unknown though the forms have an Assyrio-Babylonian cast.

The gods of Sepharvaim are handled more confidently, because children were burnt to them. Keil and Delitzsch argue from that alone that Adrammelech and Anammelech were related to Moloch, and give two possible etymologies, glorious king from the Semitic and fire-king from the Persian. Clarke takes the first for the sun and the second probably for the moon, or for the Moloch of the Ammonites. Ellicott sets both names beside well attested Assyrian gods, reading them as Adar is prince and Anu is prince.

The priesthood they improvised is described in one disputed phrase. Clarke takes of the lowest of them at face value, since one priest could not serve so mixed a population and the office was neither respectable nor lucrative, so that only the lowest would enter it. Ellicott renders it of all orders, or promiscuously, and finds in that a further sign that it was Jeroboam's mode of worship being restored, the men so made being high-place priests as opposed to priests of the temple. Keil and Delitzsch agree that Jehovah was now worshipped in the high-place temples according to the instructions of the priest the king had sent, and Wesley observes that the sacrificing taught must have been to the true God, since for their own gods they needed no instruction and would have allowed no outsider to minister. Gill sums the result in four words, that they worshipped both.
34:
The closing verdict is hard to pin to a subject, and each commentator pins it differently. Keil and Delitzsch take the former customs to be only the usages introduced when the new inhabitants settled, the ones just described, so that the sentence is about the colonists. Ellicott thinks the writer has in view the remnant of the ten tribes who amalgamated with the settlers, and later identifies the they who did not hearken plainly as the Ephraimites, clinging to the long established worship of the calves. Keil and Delitzsch divide the last verse of that pair between the two groups, the not hearkening belonging to the ten tribes and the continuing in the old manner to the Israelites left in the land. Gill leaves three readings open without choosing: the colonists keeping their own former customs, or keeping those of the idolatrous Israelites, or the captives themselves unreformed by their troubles.

That they feared the Lord and did not fear him is the paradox the chapter ends on. Ellicott resolves it by degree, that they did not fear him in the sense of a right fear, nor honour him in the way the law prescribes, and notes that the Greek drops both negatives from the verse. Wesley presses the same point harder: whatever they pretended, they worshipped their own calves and inventions, and God will not accept the mongrel worship offered him alongside. He finds the proof of it in their conduct, since men who live in the constant breach of the statutes cannot be said to fear the lawgiver, and he reads the name Israel here as an aggravation, a name given for a special interest in God and inherited by a posterity that disgraced it.

The covenant is recited at length because it is the standard being applied. Gill locates it at Sinai and observes that the first table, which the recital chiefly concerns, forbids the worship of any other god. Ellicott notices that the prohibition of fearing other gods is repeated three times over in these verses, and takes it for the main point of the covenant between Jehovah and Israel; at the promise of deliverance he marks the pronoun as emphatic, that he on his part will deliver them. Clarke takes the central verse apart into three things: the object of worship, Jehovah the supreme and self-existent Being; the reason for it, that he had saved them by a power plainly irresistible; and the manner of it, which he finds in the three verbs, reverence for the lawgiver, the bowing of the knee in humility, and sacrifice, in which a man confesses that he has sinned and deserves the death the victim dies.

How far unto this day reaches is the last thing disputed, and the answers are centuries apart. Clarke argues the notice must have been written before the Babylonish captivity, since after that none of the Israelites ever lapsed into idolatry, and allows that it may chiefly describe the heathen settled among the remains of the ten tribes. Ellicott counts generations instead: Ephraim went into captivity in 721, and the children and children's children of the verse bring us two generations on, to the exile of Judah and the age of the last editor of these books. Keil and Delitzsch say only that the mixed worship lasted until the books of the Kings were written. Wesley stretches it furthest, above three hundred years, to the time of Alexander the Great, when the Samaritans were at last prevailed upon to cast their idols away. Gill closes where the chapter began, that these nations did exactly what Israel had done before them, serving the Lord and their images together as Israel had served God and the calves.
